stem: A media company keeps 1.2 billion click events in a Delta table. After feature encoding the training set is far larger than the memory of the biggest node type available, and a churn-style logistic regression must be retrained nightly on the full history. Scoring later runs on the same Spark cluster. Which training approach fits these constraints?

choices.text: Move the job to a single-node cluster and enlarge the swap space, so the whole training set can be paged in and fitted by scikit-learn
Train scikit-learn on a 0.1% random sample, because the rare customer segments in the business requirements are not needed for the model
Build a Spark ML `Pipeline` ending in `LogisticRegression` and fit it on the DataFrame so the rows stay partitioned across the workers
Call `toPandas()` on the full training DataFrame and fit scikit-learn `LogisticRegression` on the driver, using the largest driver type available

stem: A pricing team has a 3 GB table of features. Their best model so far is a scikit-learn `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` tuned by hand, and no Spark ML regressor has matched its error on this data. The team asks whether to rewrite training as a Spark ML pipeline "because the platform is Spark". What should the ML engineer recommend?

choices.text: Convert the model to a Spark ML `LinearRegression`, because linear models are the only family that can be trained on Spark clusters
Rewrite it as a Spark ML `GBTRegressor` on a 16-worker cluster, since distributed training is faster for tree ensembles
Keep scikit-learn but run `fit` inside a `mapInPandas` call so that the data is split over the workers and each worker trains a part of the model
Keep scikit-learn on a single-node cluster, prepare features in Spark and read them with `toPandas()`, and move to Spark ML if the data outgrows memory

stem: A Spark ML `RandomForestClassifier` is fitted on a 60 GB Delta table on a cluster with 10 workers of 16 cores. The Spark UI shows only 8 tasks in the training stages while 152 cores are idle, and the fit takes far longer than the team expected. The DataFrame was read from a table stored in 8 large files. What is the most effective change?

choices.text: Switch to scikit-learn on the driver, because Spark ML cannot use more cores than the number of input files in a Delta table
Repartition the training DataFrame to a small multiple of the total core count (for example 320) and cache it before calling `fit`
Raise `spark.driver.memory` so that the driver can hold the partitions that the 8 tasks are processing, which frees the other cores
Increase `numTrees` to 160 so that Spark ML creates one task per tree and fills the idle cores with work

stem: A 1 TB Delta table feeds a gradient-boosted tree model. A learning curve shows validation error flat once the training set exceeds roughly 2% of the rows (about 20 GB), and the team has a tuned XGBoost model for this problem. Spark ML training on the full table takes hours on a large cluster. Which plan is the best trade-off?

choices.text: Sample about 5% of the rows with Spark, train the tuned XGBoost model on a single large node, and re-check the curve when the data changes
Split the table by month and train 24 separate Spark ML models, then average their predictions, which makes each fit smaller
Add more workers to the Spark ML job until the full-data run takes minutes, and accept the higher cost because only the runtime was a concern
Train the Spark ML `GBTClassifier` on all 1 TB, since more rows can only improve the model and the cluster is already paid for

stem: After a scikit-learn `RandomForestClassifier(n_jobs=-1)` job moved from a single-node cluster to a cluster with one driver and 16 workers, the training time did not change at all and the worker CPU utilization stays near zero. What explains this?

choices.text: The Delta table was read with too few partitions, so the workers were never scheduled; repartitioning to 16 would spread the fit
`n_jobs=-1` limits scikit-learn to one process per Spark executor, and the executors must first be restarted
The workers are not attached to the notebook until `spark.conf.set("spark.ml.distributed", "true")` is set
scikit-learn runs in the Python process of the driver, so only the driver cores are used and the workers have no part of the fit

stem: A team compares two prototypes on a 5 GB table: scikit-learn on a single-node cluster trains in 40 seconds, while the same algorithm in Spark ML on 10 workers takes 6 minutes. Management asks whether Spark ML is just configured badly. Which explanation is most accurate?

choices.text: For data that fits in memory, fixed costs of distributed training (task scheduling, shuffles, network aggregation) can dominate, so one node is faster
The result shows that the 10 workers are too small, and doubling the cluster would bring Spark ML below the single-node time at this data size
Spark ML uses only the driver for tree algorithms, so adding workers cannot reduce the runtime at any data size
Spark ML always reads the data twice as often as scikit-learn, so it is expected to be slower at every data size and cluster size

stem: A 200-million-row churn table has nulls in `income` and `tenure_months`. The `VectorAssembler` stage fails on them, and the first fix, filtering the null rows before training, would also drop a large share of new customers. Scoring batches contain nulls as well. How should the pipeline be changed?

choices.text: Fill the nulls with `df.fillna(0)` in the training notebook, then repeat the same call in each scoring job
Add an `Imputer(strategy="median")` stage before `VectorAssembler`, so medians learned at `fit` are stored in the model
Compute the mean of each column with `agg` on the training table and write it into a SQL expression in every consumer
Set the `VectorAssembler` option `handleInvalid` to skip, then accept that scoring batches return fewer rows than were sent in and rejoin them

stem: The feature `ctr = clicks / impressions` is added with `df.withColumn("ctr", ...)` in the training notebook, and the logistic regression pipeline is fitted on the result. The scoring team receives the saved `PipelineModel` and finds the model fails because `ctr` is missing from the raw tables. How should the training code be changed so the logic travels with the model?

choices.text: Write `ctr` to the raw table in a nightly job for all consumers
Document the formula in the model description so that each consuming team can add the column before scoring
Add a first `SQLTransformer` stage (`SELECT *, clicks / impressions AS ctr FROM __THIS__`) so the model computes it
Create a Python UDF in the scoring job that computes `ctr`, and register it under the same name as the column

stem: A text pipeline produces TF-IDF vectors with 8 million dimensions, stored as sparse vectors of about 150 non-zero values each. Linear models on them need features on a comparable scale, and a trial with `StandardScaler(withMean=True)` ran out of executor memory. Which stage keeps the vectors sparse and still rescales the features?

choices.text: `StandardScaler(withMean=True)` with a higher executor memory setting, since centering is needed for every linear model
`MinMaxScaler`, because mapping each feature to the range 0 to 1 leaves all the zeros in place
`RobustScaler(withCentering=True)`, because removing the median is cheaper than removing the mean
`MaxAbsScaler`, which divides each feature by its largest absolute value and does not center the data

stem: A pipeline for a streaming source has stages `[VectorAssembler(inputCols=["emb", "amount"]), classifier]`, where `emb` is a `VectorUDT` column produced by an upstream step. Fitting on historical batch data works, but starting the query that applies the `PipelineModel` to the streaming DataFrame fails because the size of `emb` is unknown. Which stage solves this?

choices.text: A `VectorSizeHint(inputCol="emb", size=64)` stage placed before the `VectorAssembler`
A `VectorSlicer` on `emb` with the indices 0 to 63, which fixes the size by selecting a subset of values
A `Normalizer` on `emb`, because normalizing a vector also writes the vector length into the column metadata
A `.cache()` call on the streaming DataFrame, so that Spark can look at the contents of `emb` and infer the vector size

stem: Several models (churn, upsell, support risk) share one featurization: indexing four categorical columns, one-hot encoding them, and assembling a vector. The team wants one reusable, fitted artifact for the shared featurization and separate model stages per use case. Which design applies Spark ML correctly?

choices.text: Fit the shared stages once with `fit` and call `collect()` on the result, then rebuild a `Pipeline` per model from the collected rows
Build a featurization `Pipeline` and use it as the first stage of each model `Pipeline`, since a `Pipeline` is itself an `Estimator`
Replace the shared stages by a `PipelineModel` object in the stage list of each model pipeline after calling `fit`
Create three copies of the same stage objects and put one copy into each `Pipeline`, because a stage instance may be used in only one pipeline

stem: A weekly job refits a whole `Pipeline` (`StringIndexer` on `merchant_category`, then a model) and also writes the indexed column to a Delta feature table that other teams read. After a refit, an older downstream model started producing wrong predictions, although the indexer code did not change. What is the most robust fix?

choices.text: Increase `maxCategories` on the indexer so that it learns every category and keeps the old indices stable
Refit the indexer on 10% of the data, because indices only depend on the sample size, not on the content
Store the raw category in the shared table and apply each model's own fitted `PipelineModel` at read time, so the mapping matches
Set `stringOrderType="alphabetAsc"` on the indexer, which keeps indices identical across refits even when new categories appear in the data

stem: A support-ticket model must predict the priority labels "low", "medium" and "high" stored as strings. Fitting a `LogisticRegression` on the string label column fails, and downstream reports need the original strings in the prediction output. Which stages solve both needs?

choices.text: A `Bucketizer` with splits at 1 and 2 on the label column, then a Python dictionary applied in the reporting job for the strings and a manual check
A `cast("int")` on the label column, and a stored lookup table maintained by hand for the report
A `StringIndexer` on the label, then an `IndexToString` stage after the classifier that maps `prediction` back
A `OneHotEncoder` on the label column, then reading the largest element of its vector as the prediction

stem: A feature `age` must become five bins. The business wants bins with roughly equal numbers of customers in the training data, learned once and reused unchanged when scoring later batches. Which stage fits?

choices.text: `Binarizer` applied five times with different thresholds, each producing one bin indicator
`QuantileDiscretizer(numBuckets=5)`, which learns quantile splits and returns a fixed `Bucketizer`
`StandardScaler`, because z-scores split in the same way as quantiles
`Bucketizer` with splits computed again on each scoring batch, so the bins always follow the current customer population

stem: A text classifier uses `Tokenizer`, then either `HashingTF` or `CountVectorizer`, then `IDF`, then logistic regression. Reviewers require a report of the ten words with the largest positive weights for each class, and the corpus has several million distinct terms. Which choice satisfies the requirement?

choices.text: `CountVectorizer` with a limited `vocabSize` and `minDF`, because its fitted model stores the vocabulary so that coefficient positions map back to words
`HashingTF` with `numFeatures` of 2^10, because the hashing trick keeps the vocabulary and gives each word a readable name
`HashingTF` with a very large `numFeatures`, because with enough buckets the hash index can be inverted to the word with no extra information
Neither; `IDF` already keeps the term names, so either vectorizer works and the report can be produced from the `IDF` model

stem: A team tunes a Spark ML `ALS` recommender with `CrossValidator` and `RegressionEvaluator(metricName="rmse")`. Every candidate returns an RMSE of `NaN`, so no best model can be chosen. Validation folds contain users and items that never appeared in the training folds. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Increase `rank` to 200 so that the factors cover the unseen users and items
Set `nonnegative=True` on `ALS`, which constrains factors and so prevents NaN predictions for unknown users and items
Switch the evaluator to `mae`, which ignores NaN predictions
Set `coldStartStrategy="drop"` on `ALS`, so NaN prediction rows are removed before the metric is computed

stem: A marketing team clusters customers with Spark ML `KMeans` on `annual_income` (range 20,000 to 400,000) and `visits_per_month` (range 0 to 30). The clusters turn out to be almost only income bands. What change addresses the cause?

choices.text: Replace `KMeans` with `LogisticRegression`, which handles features on different scales and groups customers automatically
Raise `maxIter` to 500 so that the algorithm eventually weights the visit counts
Add a `StandardScaler` stage on the assembled vector before `KMeans`, so both features contribute comparably to distances
Increase `k` until the visit counts start to split the clusters

stem: A genomics model uses 8,000 continuous features and a categorical label with 4 classes. The team wants a Spark ML stage that keeps the 200 features most associated with the label before training a random forest. Which stage and settings apply?

choices.text: `PCA` with `k=200`, since principal components are the 200 original features with the highest scores
`UnivariateFeatureSelector` with `featureType="continuous"`, `labelType="categorical"` (ANOVA F-test) and `numTopFeatures` selection of 200
`ChiSqSelector`, because the features are continuous and it computes a correlation between each feature and the label before the forest
`VarianceThresholdSelector` with the label column as input, which keeps the features that vary most with the label

stem: A fraud model is tuned with `CrossValidator(numFolds=5)`. Each customer has many transactions, and cross-validation scores are far higher than the scores on later customers. The team suspects the folds. What change is the best fix?

choices.text: Add a fold column such as `abs(hash(customer_id)) % 5` and pass it with `setFoldCol("fold")`
Set the seed of the `CrossValidator` so the same random folds are used for every parameter combination and run
Switch to `TrainValidationSplit(trainRatio=0.8)`, which splits at random and so avoids sharing customers
Raise `numFolds` to 20 so that each validation fold is smaller

stem: A `CrossValidator` runs a random forest grid on 4 workers of 16 cores each. A single forest fit on the 400 GB training set already keeps all executors busy. An engineer sets `setParallelism(24)` to finish faster, but the run is no quicker and some stages fail with executor memory errors. What is the best explanation and action?

choices.text: Parallelism above 1 is not allowed for tree algorithms, which is why executors fail; set it back to 1
Parallelism only affects the validation step, so the memory errors come from a bad grid and the setting can stay at 24
Parallelism must be at least the number of workers times cores (64), because lower values leave tasks unscheduled
Parallelism fits several settings at once, so concurrent fits compete for executors and memory; use a small value

stem: A team wants to pick `k` for a Spark ML `KMeans` model on 80 million unlabeled customers. They build a `ParamGridBuilder` over `k` from 3 to 12 and need an evaluator for `TrainValidationSplit`, which picks the best `ParamMap` by the evaluator metric. There is no label column. Which evaluator fits?

choices.text: `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(metricName="f1")`, comparing the cluster index with a column of random labels
`RegressionEvaluator(metricName="rmse")` on the cluster index, since lower distance to the centre is the better fit
`BinaryClassificationEvaluator`, because each cluster is a positive class against all of the others
`ClusteringEvaluator`, which computes the silhouette score from the `features` and `prediction` columns and needs no label

stem: A gradient-boosted model has six hyperparameters with continuous ranges. A full grid would need over 15,000 combinations, and the team wants to try 40 random combinations with Spark MLlib cross-validation. Which approach works?

choices.text: Set `numFolds=40` so that `CrossValidator` evaluates 40 random subsets of the grid
Pass a `scipy` distribution object to `addGrid` for each parameter, and `CrossValidator` will then draw 40 random samples from them
Sample 40 combinations in Python, build one `ParamMap` per combination into a list, and pass the list to `setEstimatorParamMaps`
Use `ParamGridBuilder().setRandom(40)` before `build()`, which makes the builder sample the grid

stem: A demand-forecasting pipeline is tuned with `CrossValidator` on two years of daily rows. The cross-validated RMSE is excellent, but after deployment the error on the following month is twice as high. Folds were created at random. What is the most likely cause and the right change?

choices.text: The grid was too small; add more parameter combinations and keep the random folds
Random folds mix past and future days, so models train on later days; split by time and validate on a later period
The data was not shuffled before cross-validation; shuffle it again and increase `numFolds` to get a stable estimate
The evaluator is wrong; `RegressionEvaluator` cannot be used on time-ordered data

stem: A team tunes a `Pipeline` with `CrossValidator` and logs `max(cvModel.avgMetrics)` of 0.91 AUC in the model card as the expected production quality. A reviewer objects. Which practice is correct?

choices.text: Hold out a test set that is never used in tuning, evaluate `cvModel.bestModel` on it once, and report that score
Keep the maximum; the best parameter map was chosen on validation data, so its score is unbiased and can be reported
Refit the best model on the whole data and report its score on the training data, which is the largest sample
Log the average of `avgMetrics` instead of the maximum, because the maximum includes the best fold
